questions.q: What happens when you call `void log_order(Order o)` where Order is a struct containing a std::string?
options: The function receives a reference to the caller's Order — no copy is made
A full copy of the Order, including a copy of the string's character data, is made for the function
A compile error occurs because structs cannot be passed by value
Only the id field is copied
questions.explain: Passing by value creates a complete copy of the argument, including any owned data like a std::string's characters — potentially expensive for larger types.

questions.q: What is the recommended default for a function parameter that only needs to read a struct's data, not modify it?
options: Pass by value (T)
Pass by non-const reference (T&)
Pass by const reference (const T&)
Pass by double pointer (T**)
questions.explain: const T& avoids copying the argument while preventing the function from modifying the caller's object — the standard default for read-only access to anything larger than a primitive.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a reference from a pointer in C++?
options: A reference can be null; a pointer cannot
A reference must be bound when created and can never be null or rebound; a pointer can be null and reassigned
They are exactly the same thing with different syntax
A pointer is always faster than a reference
questions.explain: A reference is permanently bound to the object it was initialized with and can never be null. A pointer is more flexible — it can be null, reassigned, or point to different objects over its lifetime.

questions.q: When is it acceptable to pass a parameter by value rather than by const reference?
options: Never — const reference should always be used
When the type is small and cheap to copy, such as int, double, or bool
Only for std::string parameters
Only when the function is a member function
questions.explain: For small, cheap-to-copy types like int, double, and bool, passing by value is simple and has negligible cost. The const-reference rule matters most for larger types like structs, strings, and containers.

questions.q: In `void fill_order(Order& o, long filled_qty) { o.quantity -= filled_qty; }`, why is the parameter a plain reference instead of const?
options: It's a mistake; it should be const
const references are faster, so this is a performance bug
The function needs to modify the caller's Order object, which a const reference would not allow
Plain references are required whenever a second parameter is also present
questions.explain: Because fill_order modifies the caller's quantity field in place, it needs a non-const reference — a const reference would prevent that modification.
